questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: How to bake a traditional pasty in your own kitchen
Famous foods from Italy and New York and their history
The annual pasty competition in Cornwall and its winners
The history of the Cornish pasty and how it spread
questions.why: Neil says they'll hear how the pasty went from humble beginnings to spread around the world.

questions.q: What is the game Neil and Rob play at the start?
options: Naming the first food that comes to mind for a place
Guessing which country a famous food comes from
Naming as many different pies as possible in a minute
Guessing all the ingredients of a dish from its name
questions.why: Neil names a place and Rob says the first food that comes to mind.

questions.q: How does Rob describe a pasty?
options: A kind of pizza with meat and cheese on top
A small, sweet cake filled with fruit and cream
Between a pie and a sandwich, with folded pastry
A type of soft bread roll with butter inside
questions.why: He says it's somewhere between a pie and a sandwich, with pastry turned over and crimped.

questions.q: According to Polly Russell's early source, who were pasties made for?
options: Rich families in the city
Farm workers at harvest time
Fishermen at sea
Children at school
questions.why: She says they were made specifically for labourers on a farm at harvest time.

questions.q: According to Ruth Huxley, why did pasties become so important in Cornwall?
options: They were cheap to buy in shops
They were eaten at religious festivals
The fishing industry depended on them
They were perfect for eating down the mines
questions.why: She says it just worked perfectly down mines, and Cornwall became the world capital of mining.

questions.q: How did the pasty spread around the world?
options: Cornish chefs opened lots of restaurants abroad
Cornish miners emigrated and took the recipe along
Tourists took the recipes home after their holidays
A big company exported frozen pasties by ship
questions.why: Ruth Huxley says the mining community went all over the world and took the pasty with them.

questions.q: Which places does Polly Russell mention where similar foods are found?
options: Mexico, Minnesota, Canada and Australia
France, Spain, Italy and Portugal
China, Japan, India and Thailand
Only other parts of England and Wales
questions.why: She mentions Mexico, America, Minnesota, Canada and Australia.

questions.q: Why does Neil mention empanadas and Jamaican patties?
options: They are much older than the Cornish pasty itself
They won the World Pasty Championships last year
They are pasty-inspired foods from around the world
They are Rob's favourite foods to eat for lunch
questions.why: He calls them other pasty-inspired ideas, showing the pasty is still going strong worldwide.
